title: Stars and cards, honestly
hook: what's your sign, and the tarot card that seems to know you: the real history, the real psychology, and what they can't do
tomorrow: Ego death and the higher self

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pennebaker, and writing it out. Your line was the stone in your shoe. Day three hundred nineteen.

What's your sign? It's a first-date question, a group-chat joke, a whole app on a lot of phones. And on a hard night, maybe you pull a tarot card, and the card seems to know exactly what you're going through. Then a skeptical friend rolls their eyes, and you feel a little silly. You don't need to. There's real history here, and real psychology, and an honest answer about what the stars and the cards can and can't do. Today: stars and cards, honestly.
screen: `WHAT'S YOUR SIGN?` → `A CARD THAT SEEMS TO KNOW YOU.` → `STARS AND CARDS, HONESTLY.`

segments.voice: First, the stars. Astrology is old. In ancient Babylon, scribes read the sky for omens about kings and harvests, and the twelve signs of the zodiac took shape there. In Greek-speaking Egypt, roughly two thousand years ago, it grew into the personal horoscope: a chart of the sky at the hour you were born. Horoscope is Greek for hour-watcher. Second, the cards. Tarot began in fifteenth-century Italy as a deck for playing a card game, and people played it for centuries. Its fame for fortune-telling came later, in eighteenth-century France, when a writer claimed the cards held ancient Egyptian wisdom. There's no evidence they did. Most decks you see today follow one published in London in 1909, drawn by the artist Pamela Colman Smith. Third, the tests. In 1985 the journal Nature published a careful one: astrologers tried to match people's birth charts to their personality profiles, and did no better than chance. Back in 1949, a psychologist gave each of his students a personality reading. Every reading was the same, and they rated it as remarkably accurate. Vague, kind descriptions feel personal. That's called the Barnum effect. Fourth, why people love them anyway. A sign gives you words for yourself. A card gives you a pause, and a picture to think with. In an uncertain week, a little order is a comfort. Used as a mirror, plenty of people find that useful. As a forecast, nothing backs it, so don't hand it the big choices: a job, a breakup, your health. Ask the card a question if you like. Then ask yourself.
screen: `BABYLON'S SKY, EGYPT'S HOROSCOPE.` · `TAROT BEGAN AS A CARD GAME.` · `THE TESTS: NO BETTER THAN CHANCE.` · `A MIRROR, NOT A FORECAST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're unsure about this week. Don't pull a card; picture the card you'd most want to pull, the image that would say what you need to hear: a road, a sunrise, a door, a person? That picture came from you, so stay with what it shows you, breathing slowly.
Horoscope, Greek for hour-watcher: a chart of the sky at the hour you were born. A mirror, maybe. A forecast, no. Today's word.
Your line: a mirror, not a forecast. Enjoy the sign and the card, and keep the big choices for yourself. Day three hundred nineteen.

Facts to confirm: twelve-sign zodiac developed in Babylonia (c. 5th century BCE); personal horoscopes in Hellenistic Egypt (c. 2nd–1st century BCE), 'roughly two thousand years ago'.

Tarot: tarocchi/trionfi in 15th-century northern Italy; Antoine Court de Gébelin's Egyptian claim (1781); the Rider-Waite(-Smith) deck published by Rider in London, 1909, art by Pamela Colman Smith. 'Most decks today follow' it: a common claim; soften to 'many' if the Keeper prefers.
Carlson 1985: astrologers matched natal charts to California Psychological Inventory profiles at chance. Forer 1949: one generic sketch, average rating about 4.3 of 5. Summarized, not quoted.
